doc.title: Eddie Palmieri — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Lucumi Macumba Voodoo
summary: The Epic album, its African religious roots, Bobby Colomby's role, Francisco Aguabella and why it did not sell.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Yeah. But it was done. If it isn’t meant to happen, it isn’t meant to happen. But it was done. Just like Lucumi Macumba Voodoo. That’s another one.
Right. We’ll talk about that one.

I did it so well for Epic, they didn’t know what to do. I was in the Black Department. I don’t mean the “Black Department.” The head of the black artists. They asked me, one of my friends said, “What happened?” I said, “I guess they weren’t black enough.” They didn’t know what to do with my record.
This one was produced by Bobby Columby.
They brought him after, for like both productions.

After I had the first session that didn’t turn out well, I brought in René Hernández for a minute. I had brought René Hernández from Puerto Rico; he did a number called “A Danzon,” that never came out on that album. It came out later, on the White Album of Fania. Bobby Columby brought me another... But Bobby brought in great singers on that. We really needed him to come in, because the first attempt to record it didn’t turn out, and it cost the company a lot of money. They brought in Bobby to coordinate. And I’m glad I met him. Because of him, it turned out to be quite successful. But then I finished out the project, and I mixed it.
The title, of course, is in reference to traditional African religion.
Right. I studied the santeria. But it was Lucumi Macumba Voodoo. I figured if I
really get good into voodoo, all the people who were quite critics of me, I could have turned them into little hamsters. But it didn’t work.
But each one, Lucumi, Macumba and Voodoo... I mean, Voodoo is from Haiti, right, but they all from African...
Lucumi, African, you know. And Macumba, Brazilian.
So you’re diversified, but the root is from Africa.

Well, the idea was that it all related to the belief, the religious belief. Chango is Shango in Brazil. But the idea is that they were all captives that were brought in, and what happened to the development... I brought in the great percussionist, Francisco Aguabella. He sang there, he played the batas; it was quite accepted... As a matter of fact, my friend Manny Lopez was traveling with the Irakere, and he brought them to the studio when I was recording for CBS. They heard...Chucho Valdés heard Lucumi Macumba Voodoo. We blew them away. I mean, he just was so impressed with what he heard. But that it didn’t do well commercially, that was something else. Because they put me in Epic, and they didn’t know what to do with it. Whatever. And Puerto Rico wasn’t going to understand it. It just wasn’t going to... It just didn’t happen. But it’s there also. I am very proud of that recording.
